feedback: If a learner says only heat-sensitive animals are affected: follow one link at a time from the warmed water to a producer, then to its consumers, making the knock-on connections visible.
If a learner predicts a one-step effect only: ask them to keep going — 'and then what happens to the animals that ate that one?' — until they reach something two or more steps away.
Reinforce when a learner spontaneously names an indirect or distant effect: this is the systems-thinking goal.
Note that warming need not always thin plankton — depending on conditions it could make plankton bloom or crash — so the exact chain is one example of coupling, not a fixed rule.

If a learner expects the system to snap back automatically, discuss thresholds: small changes may be absorbed, but a big or sustained one can flip the system to a new state (kelp forest becoming an urchin barren).
activities.intendedInsight: An ocean ecosystem is living AND non-living parts locked together; changing one factor cascades through multiple steps, and effects can be indirect and surprising rather than staying contained to one species.
learnerActions: Explore a kelp-forest model with adjustable factors for water temperature, light, salinity and current, and a community of producers (phytoplankton, the plant-like plankton, and kelp), consumers (zooplankton, urchins, fish, sea otters) and decomposers.
Change ONE factor only — e.g. nudge the water warmer — and watch over time how the community responds step by step.
Before each change, predict out loud which living thing will be hit first and what will follow two or three steps along the chain.

After watching, trace the actual chain in order (for example: warmer water → plankton thin out → the plankton-feeders that ate them dwindle → their predators go hungry → decomposer workload shifts) and compare it with your prediction. Treat this as one plausible outcome, not the only one.
Run several different perturbations (e.g. cloudier water so less light gets through) and note any effect that surprised you or reached a creature you would not have connected to that factor.
State in your own words why touching just one non-living factor moved the whole web.
activities.title: Run the kelp forest: perturb one factor, trace the ripple

feedback: If a learner lists only animals and plants, prompt: 'Where do temperature, light, salinity and currents go on this map?' to show they belong inside the system.
If a learner draws only one-way arrows, ask what happens to dead matter and nutrients, guiding them to close the loop through decomposers.
activities.intendedInsight: An ecosystem's parts — living and non-living — are connected into a structure, and non-living factors are members of the system, not just a backdrop.
learnerActions: Study a labelled ecosystem web showing producers, consumers, decomposers and the non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents).
Select a non-living factor (e.g. temperature or light) and identify which organisms it affects and how.
Sketch or describe at least one first-order effect: 'if this rose, then ...'.
Add the decomposers and show how they return matter to the system, making it a cycle rather than a one-way chain.
activities.title: Map the system: living and non-living parts linked

feedback: For sorting: if temperature or light is placed outside the ecosystem, clarify that these are parts of the system, not just its setting. A sort checks classification but does not itself require the learner to trace a cascade, so pair it with the scenario step.
For the scenario: if the answer is 'only the heat-sensitive animals change', ask for the next link in the chain and the one after that.

Model answer for the warming scenario: probably not — because the parts are connected, a season of water a few degrees warmer can weaken the kelp (a producer) or make plankton bloom or crash; that can change food for the animals that eat them, which can change their predators and which species survive there, so the effect is likely to spread rather than stay contained, even though the exact chain depends on conditions.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can name the system's parts, tell a food web from an ecosystem, and follow a change through several steps rather than only naming isolated parts.
learnerActions: Sort items into living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
Name the key non-living factors that affect ocean life: temperature, salinity, light, currents.
Distinguish a food web (energy among organisms) from an ecosystem (organisms plus their physical environment as one system).
Given a scenario — e.g. the water warms a few degrees for a whole season — trace the multi-step ripple and explain whether the effect stays contained.
activities.title: Check your understanding: parts, definitions and cascades
